definition: Prolix means so tediously long-winded that the words outnumber the ideas.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word prolix. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know prolix should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The minutes of the garden society run prolix under its current secretary: last month's vote on mulch fills nine pages, complete with weather.
Chatty is friendly overflow, easily forgiven; it sits at the mild end, well short of prolix.
Wordy goes further than chatty — the sentences are now carrying fat — but prolix tops the ladder: long-windedness so tedious that readers start skipping.

Long-winded is the everyday word for taking forever to reach the point — the after-dinner speech that circles its toast for ten minutes. Prolix means the same fault in a reviewer's register, and it adds a verdict: the length has become tedious, the words outnumbering the ideas.

Rambling talk wanders off the path as well as taking too long on it — one story drifts into three others. Prolix writing can stay perfectly on its subject and still exhaust you: the fault prolix names is tedious length, not lost direction.
